newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Container ship in quasi-direct China-Taiwan voyage.
newsitem.headline: Container ship in quasi-direct China-Taiwan voyage.

text.p: A Hong Kong-owned container ship has arrived in Taiwan after an unprecedented quasi-direct passage from China via Hong Kong, a senior Taiwan transport official said on Wednesday.

"Kaohsiung port authorities have processed this ship under new rules adopted on January 22 allowing ships to transfer shipments between China and Taiwan via a third place," said Hsieh Ming-hui of Taiwan's transport ministry.
"This is consistent with the two sides' understanding reached during January negotiations in Hong Kong," said Hsieh, director of the ministry's navigation and aviation office.

Officials said it was the first such quasi-direct passage in 48 years of Taiwan-China rivalry. The container ship, the Lien Fung, arrived on February 23 from China's southeastern special economic zone at Xiamen after transiting Hong Kong harbour.
Kaohsiung is heavily industrialised Taiwan's main southern gateway and one of the world's busiest container ports.

Nationalist-ruled Taiwan and the communist mainland have been locked in a bitter and sometimes bloody ideological rivalry since the Republic of China government was defeated in a civil war in 1949 and fled into exile on the offshore island.

Despite the longtime stalemate, an easing of unofficial ties since the late 1980s has enabled 30,000 Taiwan firms to pour more than US$20 billion into investments in the booming Chinese mainland -- fuelling intense pressure for an end to Taiwan's ban on direct shipping, air travel and communications.
China froze semi-official talks in mid-1995, but officials from both sides have encouraged the private sector to continue exploring ways to forge direct or semi-direct shipping links.

With tacit official approval from both sides, shipping executives reached an understanding in Hong Kong on January 22 under which shipping companies from each side can apply to the other to mount such quasi-direct sailings via a "third place", something that at least 10 Taiwan shippers have done.
Because the "third place" is understood to be Hong Kong, the formula faces a daunting test on July 1 when the territory reverts to Chinese rule after 150 years as a British colony.
Officially, Taipei and Beijing remain divided on how direct shipping should work due to fundamental sovereignty issues.

Taiwan has proposed in that direct sailings involve only ships flying third-country flags and that mainland-sourced cargoes be handled at "offshore transshipment centres" elsewhere in Asia or in Taiwan but outside Taiwan customs.
All major Taiwan shippers have ships registered overseas.
Beijing, which sees Taiwan as a rebel-held part of its territory, issued rules in 1996 calling China-Taiwan shipping a domestic matter -- an approach at odds with Taiwan's plan.
One industry analyst said Taiwan could use Hong Kong as its offshore transshipment centre under a broad interpretation of Taiwan's rules.
"Taiwan can try to expand its interpretation of rules to include Hong Kong as its transshipment centre," he said.

It was not immediately known whether Beijing issued permits allowing the Lien Fung to make the Xiamen-Kaohsiung passage via Hong Kong. If such permission was issued, other shippers could be expected to try such crossings, analysts said.
